articles.title: microRNAs in Cerebrovascular Disease.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are major causes of morbidity and mortality in developed countries. Cerebrovascular diseases, especially stroke, represent major burden of disability and economy impact. Major advances in primary and secondary prevention and therapy are needed in order to tackle this public health problem. Our better understanding of pathophysiology is essential in order to develop novel diagnostic and therapeutic tools and strategies. microRNAs are a family of important post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression and their involvement in the pathophysiology of cerebrovascular diseases has already been reported. Moreover, microRNAs may represent above-mentioned potential diagnostic and therapeutic tools in clinical practice. Within this chapter, we briefly describe basic epidemiology, aetiology and clinical manifestation of following cerebrovascular diseases: extracranial carotid atherosclerosis, acute stroke, intracranial aneurysms and cerebral arterio-venous malformations. Further, in each chapter, the current knowledge about the involvement of specific microRNAs and their potential use in clinical practice will be summarized. More specifically, within the subchapter "miRNAs in carotid atherosclerosis", general information about miRNA involvement in atherosclerosis will be described (miR-126, miR-17-92, miR-155 and others) with special emphasis put on miRNAs affecting carotid plaque progression and stability (e.g. miR-145, miR-146 or miR-217). In the subchapter "miRNAs in acute stroke", we will provide insight into recent knowledge from animal and human studies concerning miRNA profiling in acute stroke and their expression dynamics in brain tissue and extracellular fluids (roles of, e.g. let-7 family, miR-21, miR-29 family, miR-124, miR-145, miR-181 family, miR-210 and miR-223). Subchapters dealing with "miRNAs and AV malformations" and "miRNAs and intracranial aneurysms" will focus on miR-21, miR-26, miR-29 family and miR-143/145.

articles.title: Endovascular Treatment for Acute Type B Aortic Dissection Involving a Right-sided Aortic Arch and Kommerell's Diverticulum: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aortic dissection involving a right-sided aortic arch (RAA) associated with Kommerell's diverticulum is extremely rare and remains a complicated entity for surgical therapy because of its anatomical characteristics. Fewer than 40 cases have been reported in the English language literature to date.
METHODS: We reported a case of 69-year-old male patient who presented with acute type B aortic dissection involving an RAA associated with Kommerell's diverticulum, a stent-graft was accurately deployed and embolization of the left subclavian artery. In addition, a review of the literature was performed to examine its clinical presentation and the efficacy of management strategies.
RESULTS: One year follow-up showed positive aortic remodeling with exclusion of Kommerell's diverticulum and thrombosis of the false lumen.
CONCLUSIONS: An aortic dissection involving an RAA associated with Kommerell's diverticulum is an extremely rare condition. Endovascular therapy is technically feasible when the dissection involves this unusual vascular malformation.

articles.title: Vascular malformations revisited.
articles.abstract: Vascular malformations are congenital anomalies that can affect each part of the vasculature. Combined forms are common and they are often part of complex syndromes. Most malformations are diagnosed during infancy, but some get obvious only later in life. The field of vascular malformations is emerging with recently described new entities and treatments. Still, misdiagnosis is common in this field, leading to nosologic confusion and wrong treatment. Clinical evaluation and imaging are the gold standard for diagnostic confirmation. Sclerotherapy and embolization are the main treatment techniques but are also used preoperatively to reduce blood loss and shrink the lesion if surgery is planned. Despite new treatment options, especially if extensive in size or involving vulnerable structures, vascular malformations are still considered chronic diseases and cause significant morbidity. Common understanding and agreement on terminology and a multidisciplinary approach are the basis of successful treatment and long-term support for these patients. Continuing research in the field of vascular anomalies will improve knowledge and create further treatment options.

articles.title: Imaging of vascular lesions of the head and neck.
articles.abstract: The diagnosis of vascular lesions of the head and neck should be directed by classifying the lesions as tumors or malformations and by determining their flow characteristics. Location of the lesion is key when differentiating between vascular neoplasms. Ultrasonography is an appropriate screening tool; MRI is often used to confirm the diagnosis. Computed tomography can be used for further characterization of the lesion, particularly when there is bony involvement. In many cases, vascular lesions grow to be extensive. In these cases, percutaneous sclerotherapy or embolization therapy can be employed to aid in surgical resection.

articles.title: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome: a case report and literature review.
articles.abstract: Blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome (BRBNS) is a rare disease characterized by multiple venous malformations and hemangiomas in the skin and visceral organs. The lesions often involve the cutaneous and gastrointestinal systems. Other organs can also be involved, such as the central nervous system, liver, and muscles. The most common symptoms are gastrointestinal bleeding and secondary iron deficiency anemia. The syndrome may also present with severe complications such as rupture, intestinal torsion, and intussusception, and can even cause death. Cutaneous malformations are usually asymptomatic and do not require treatment. The treatment of gastrointestinal lesions is determined by the extent of intestinal involvement and severity of the disease. Most patients respond to supportive therapy, such as iron supplementation and blood transfusion. For more significant hemorrhages or severe complications, surgical resection, endoscopic sclerosis, and laser photocoagulation have been proposed. Here we present a case of BRBNS in a 45-year-old woman involving 16 sites including the scalp, eyelid, orbit, lip, tongue, face, back, upper and lower limbs, buttocks, root of neck, clavicle area, superior mediastinum, glottis, esophagus, colon, and anus, with secondary severe anemia. In addition, we summarize the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, differential diagnosis and therapies of this disease by analyzing all previously reported cases to enhance the awareness of this syndrome.

articles.title: Current views on diagnostic approach and treatment of lymphedema.
articles.abstract: Lymphedema is a chronic, progressive, and often debilitating condition. Primary lymphedema is a lymphatic malformation developing during the later stage of lymphangiogenesis. Secondary lymphedema is the result of obstruction or disruption of the lymphatic system, which can occur as a consequence of tumors, surgery, trauma, infection, inflammation, and radiation therapy. In this review, we report an update upon the diagnostic approach and the medical and surgical therapy for both primary and secondary lymphedema.

articles.title: Macrocephaly-capillary malformation syndrome: description of a case and review of clinical diagnostic criteria.
articles.abstract: Macrocephaly-capillary malformation (M-CM) is characterized by prenatal overgrowth, variable somatic and cerebral asymmetry, primary megalencephaly, characteristic facial features, an abnormal neurocognitive profile and cutaneous vascular malformations. It was previously known under the name macrocephaly-cutis marmorata telangiectatica congenital (M-CMTC). However a recent review of the previously reported cases has suggested that the vascular anomalies are not true CMTC but rather capillary malformations. The diagnosis is primary clinical and different criteria have been proposed for this purpose. However, M-CM is frequently associated with structural brain abnormalities that should be properly investigated and monitored because of their possible progressive development. We report the neuroradiological and morphological features observed in a girl with M-CM and we compared them with proposed diagnostic criteria found in the literature.

articles.title: Vascular and perivascular lesions of skin and soft tissues in children and adolescents.
articles.abstract: Vascular anomalies in children and adolescents are the most common soft tissue lesions and include reactive, malformative, and neoplastic tumefactions, with a full spectrum of benign, intermediate, and malignant neoplasms. These lesions are diagnostically challenging because of morphologic complexity and recent changes in classification systems, some of which are based on clinical features and others on pathologic findings. In recent decades, there have been significant advances in clinical diagnosis, development of new therapies, and a better understanding of the genetic aspects of vascular biology and syndromes that include unusual vascular proliferations. Most vascular lesions in children and adolescents are benign, although the intermediate locally aggressive and intermediate rarely metastasizing neoplasms are important to distinguish from benign and malignant mimics. Morphologic recognition of a vasoproliferative lesion is straightforward in most instances, and conventional morphology remains the cornerstone for a specific diagnosis. However, pathologic examination is enhanced by adjunctive techniques, especially immunohistochemistry to characterize the type of vessels involved. Multifocality may cause some uncertainty regarding the assignment of "benign" or "malignant." However, increased interest in vascular anomalies, clinical expertise, and imaging technology have contributed greatly to our understanding of these disorders to the extent that in most vascular malformations and in many tumors, a diagnosis is made clinically and biopsy is not required for diagnosis. The importance of close collaboration between the clinical team and the pathologist cannot be overemphasized. For some lesions, a diagnosis is not possible from evaluation of histopathology alone, and in a subset of these, a specific diagnosis may not be possible even after all assembled data have been reviewed. In such instances, a consensus diagnosis in conjunction with clinical colleagues guides therapy. The purpose of this review is to delineate the clinicopathologic features of vascular lesions in children and adolescents with an emphasis on their unique aspects, use of diagnostic adjuncts, and differential diagnosis.

articles.title: Current concepts of vascular anomalies.
articles.abstract: The field of vascular anomalies is confusing because numerous types of lesions exist, different anomalies often look similar, and imprecise terminology commonly is used. Pharmacotherapy is effective for certain vascular tumors; sclerotherapy generally is the primary treatment of problematic lymphatic and venous malformations. Arteriovenous malformations remain difficult to manage because of their high progression and recurrence rates. Propranolol has gained popularity recently for the treatment of problematic infantile hemangioma, but its efficacy and safety compared with corticosteroid therapy have not been studied. Continuing education is needed to increase the use of accepted biologic terms to describe vascular anomalies; this will improve patient care and facilitate research. As vascular anomalies centers continue to develop, children will have easier access to interdisciplinary expertise. Patients are most likely to be diagnosed and treated properly when managed by a specialist or team focused on these conditions. Recent insight into the etiopathogenesis of infantile hemangioma and vascular malformations may lead to novel therapies for these lesions in the near future.

articles.title: Maternal immunoglobulin G anti-A and anti-B antibody titres for predicting neonatal immune sensitisation in ABO-incompatible pregnancies: The Maternal Anti-A and Anti-B Antibody Titres in ABO-Incompatible Pregnancies study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Maternal immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti-A and anti-B antibodies can cross the placenta and cause ABO haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (ABO-HDFN). We aimed to evaluate whether maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres predict neonatal direct antiglobulin test (DAT) positivity in ABO-incompatible pregnancies.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this prospective observational cohort study, 889 consecutive ABO-incompatible mother-newborn pairs were enrolled between November 2025 and June 2026. Maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres were measured after 0.01 M dithiothreitol treatment using the conventional tube antiglobulin titration method. Neonatal ABO grouping and DAT were performed by column agglutination technology. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and multivariable logistic regression assessed the predictive performance of maternal antibody titres.
RESULTS: Overall, 112/889 (12.6%) neonates were DAT positive. Maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres were significantly higher in mothers of DAT-positive neonates (both p < 0.001). Maternal IgG anti-A (area under the curve [AUC] 0.778) and anti-B (AUC 0.803) showed acceptable diagnostic performance. Higher thresholds (anti-A ≥32; anti-B ≥16) achieved 100% specificity, whereas lower thresholds (anti-A ≥8; anti-B ≥4) provided high sensitivity for excluding neonatal DAT positivity. Increasing maternal IgG anti-A (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.12, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.06-1.18) and anti-B titres (aOR 1.18, 95% CI: 1.09-1.28) independently predicted DAT positivity (both p < 0.001). Most DAT-positive neonates required phototherapy (94.6%) but none required exchange transfusion.
CONCLUSION: Standardised maternal IgG anti-A and anti-B titres independently could predict neonatal DAT positivity. A dual-threshold approach may complement existing antenatal assessment by identifying high-risk pregnancies and guiding individualised postnatal surveillance.

articles.title: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy in Acute Liver Failure: Rationale, Evidence, and Evolving Practice.
articles.abstract: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a life-threatening condition hallmarked by an acute onset of liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and encephalopathy in individuals without pre-existing liver disease. Advances in intensive care, coupled with increased access to liver transplant (LT), have substantially improved outcomes of individuals with ALF. Aggressive goal-directed intensive care focusing on individual organs has become the cornerstone of ALF management. In this context, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) has emerged as a critical component in the management of ALF. While traditionally centered around providing renal support and optimizing renal injury, the use of CRRT in ALF has expanded to include potential benefits in controlling intracranial hypertension, managing volume status and metabolic abnormalities, and reducing hyperammonemia. The use of CRRT for nonrenal ALF-centric indications has gradually gained credence. This review examines the mechanistic aspects and principles of CRRT in ALF, summarizing current clinical evidence and practice patterns. We delve into aspects of basic circuit knowledge, timing of initiation, targets of therapy, challenges of anticoagulation, emerging literature on the combination of plasma exchange with CRRT, and provide insights into pragmatic decision-making with CRRT in ALF. Lastly, the review focuses on endpoints for the use of CRRT in ALF, as well as associated challenges and future directions.

articles.title: Late-onset pneumocystis pneumonia after kidney transplantation: A systematic review and meta-analysis of prevalence, risk factors, and outcomes.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Late-onset Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is increasingly recognized in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) despite widespread prophylaxis. However, its prevalence and risk factors remain unclear.
METHODS: We systematically searched electronic databases for studies published up to May 1, 2025, that reported prevalence or risk factors of late-onset PCP. Pooled prevalence, weighted mean differences (WMDs), and pooled odds ratios (ORs) were synthesized using a random-effects model.
RESULTS: Of 1448 studies screened, 24 met inclusion criteria, comprising 57,662 KTRs, of whom 556 developed late-onset PCP. The pooled prevalence was 1.28 % (95 %CI 0.90-1.65). Lymphocyte counts were significantly lower in the infection group (WMD -408.34 cells/μL; 95 %CI -706.03 to -110.66). Risk was significantly increased with ABO-incompatible transplantation (OR 4.12; 95 %CI 1.04-16.30), rituximab induction (OR 4.77; 95 %CI, 1.50-15.21), corticosteroid (OR 2.56; 95 %CI 1.00-6.52) or mammalian target of rapamycin inhibitor (mTORi) maintenance (OR 2.37; 95 %CI 1.27-4.42), CMV infection (OR 5.21; 95 %CI 2.45-11.10), and rejection episodes (OR 2.93; 95 %CI 1.72-4.99), particularly when treated with plasma exchange, intravenous methylprednisolone, or rituximab. In contrast, cotrimoxazole prophylaxis reduced risk (OR 0.06; 95 %CI 0.01-0.60). Late-onset PCP was associated with graft loss (OR 6.11; 95 %CI 2.98-12.55) and mortality (OR 10.48; 95 %CI 1.92-57.16).
CONCLUSIONS: Although uncommon, late-onset PCP in KTRs is strongly linked with ABO-incompatible transplantation, lack of cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, lymphopenia, CMV infection, corticosteroid and mTORi, and rejection. KTRs with these high-risk features, including those receiving mTORi and corticosteroid maintenance, should be considered for prolonged or life-long PCP prophylaxis.

articles.title: Innovations to Improve Survival in Acute Liver Failure.
articles.abstract: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a medical emergency with high mortality rates. Liver transplantation is the optimal treatment for eligible patients. However, it necessitates access to transplantation services, significant financial resources, and frequently poses challenges in ensuring safe transportation. Advances in intensive care have improved survival rates from 20% to over 60%. Key factors include early prognostication, dynamic modeling, neurocritical monitoring, and liver support systems. There is a significant need for better public health services for preventing and managing ALF in India, highlighting the importance of innovative healthcare delivery and algorithm-based care. Recent advancements in liver support systems, novel pharmacological approaches, and enhanced critical care protocols can improve transplant-free survival in ALF. Innovative strategies like early and accessible plasma exchange (PLEX) for rodenticide poisoning-related ALF in Tamil Nadu have offered hope for improving public health services to provide innovative therapeutics in resource-constrained settings. This comprehensive review aims to explore the latest advancements in the management of ALF covering pathobiology, prognostic scores and biomarkers, noninvasive monitoring of intracranial hypertension (optic nerve sheath diameter and transcranial Doppler) and the use of modalities such as PLEX, and continuous renal replacement therapy. We highlight advancements and explore future innovations to enhance outcomes for individuals with ALF. Additionally, we address epidemiological changes in ALF in India and the associated challenges for healthcare policy.

articles.title: Recent Progress in Double Filtration Plasmapheresis.
articles.abstract: Double-filtration plasmapheresis is an advanced extracorporeal blood purification technique that selectively removes pathogenic macromolecules based on molecular weight. Unlike conventional plasma exchange, double-filtration plasmapheresis uses a two-step filtration process to retain beneficial plasma components such as albumin, while eliminating harmful substances, thereby reducing the need for exogenous plasma replacement. Over the last few decades, double-filtration plasmapheresis has gained prominence in the management of refractory autoimmune, neurological, metabolic, and renal diseases. This review systematically examines the therapeutic mechanisms, recent clinical advances, safety, limitations, and prospects of double-filtration plasmapheresis.

articles.title: Targeting the Calcium-mtDNA-cGAS-STING Signaling Nexus: A Novel Redox Mechanism for Nimodipine's Neuroprotection in Traumatic Brain Injury.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) induces severe secondary injury where molecular mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigates the involvement of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway in this process and evaluates the neuroprotective effect of the L-type calcium channel blocker nimodipine, focusing on calcium homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and inflammatory signaling.
METHODS: Using primary neuronal and mouse TBI models, we assessed outcomes via fluorescent calcium imaging, JC-1 staining, Western blot, quantitative PCR (qPCR)/reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and behavioral tests. Nimodipine was applied to inhibit L-type channels, specifically testing its role in reducing mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) release, blocking cGAS-STING activation, and suppressing neuroinflammation.
RESULTS: TBI markedly activated the cGAS-STING pathway, increasing pro-inflammatory factors and apoptosis. In the cellular oxygen-glucose deprivation model, calcium overload was directly observed by Fluo-4 AM staining and was associated with subsequent mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening and mtDNA release, identifying this process as a key upstream event for cGAS-STING activation. Nimodipine inhibited intracellular calcium overload, reduced mitochondrial injury and mtDNA release, and consequently suppressed cGAS-STING pathway activation. Both in vivo and in vitro experiments showed dose-dependent decreases in pro-inflammatory factors, along with improved neurological function and attenuated brain tissue pathology.
CONCLUSION: Nimodipine attenuates secondary neuroinflammation and neuronal apoptosis after TBI by inhibiting calcium influx, decreasing mtDNA release, and suppressing cGAS-STING signaling. These results suggest that the Ca2+-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis contributes to TBI pathology and that nimodipine may serve as a potential multitarget therapy. Antioxid. Redox Signal. 00, 000-000.

articles.title: Stroke-associated pneumonia: from immunodepression to bedside management and future research directions.
articles.abstract: Stroke-associated pneumonia (SAP) is one of the most frequent complications after acute stroke, affecting approximately one in eight stroke patients. Besides prolonged hospitalisation and increased healthcare costs, it is also a major risk factor for mortality and poor functional recovery. The pathophysiology of SAP is driven by two converging processes: impaired local airway defence due to dysphagia as well as reduced airway clearance reflexes, and systemic stroke-induced immunodepression driven by dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system. While post-stroke immunodepression is a major risk factor for SAP, it might limit unwanted autoimmune responses within the brain. Conversely, SAP itself may drive neuroinflammation and contribute to post-stroke cognitive impairment. Despite its clinical importance, high-quality evidence to guide practice on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of SAP remains scarce and guideline recommendations are mostly based on expert consensus. Diagnosis of SAP is suggested to be based on standardised clinical criteria supported by chest radiography and C-reactive protein as an adjunct where uncertainty persists. After diagnosis, guidelines suggest prompt empirical antibiotic therapy according to local protocols. In contrast, preventive antibiotics, even for high-risk patients, neither improve clinical outcome nor reduce SAP frequency. Currently recommended preventive strategies for SAP therefore mostly focus on dysphagia management and early mobilisation. This review integrates the pathophysiology, long-term consequences of SAP and further research directions based on the current knowledge on post-stroke immunology with prevention, diagnosis and treatment of SAP as set out in the recent European Stroke Organisation guideline and related guidelines.

articles.title: Analysis of multidimensional molecular mechanisms in Parkinson's disease and precise therapeutic strategies.
articles.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common neurodegenerative disorder worldwide, is characterized by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and striatal dopamine deficiency, leading to motor dysfunction. The complex pathogenesis involves impaired protein homeostasis with α-synuclein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation, including NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Newly identified regulated cell death pathways - including ferroptosis, cuproptosis, pyroptosis, and necroptosis - have further expanded current understanding of PD pathology, while gut-brain axis interactions may contribute to peripheral-central communication and disease progression. These mechanistic insights inspire targeted therapeutic strategies comprising α-synuclein inhibitors, mitochondrial protectants, anti-inflammatory agents, and novel cell death pathway blockers, alongside gut-brain axis interventions. However, these approaches face substantial challenges including limited blood-brain barrier penetration, insufficient target specificity, and individual genetic heterogeneity. Future research should prioritize developing multi-target combination therapies, integrating multi-omics and computational approaches for biomarker identification and patient stratification, while advancing clinical translation of gene- and cell-based therapies. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and precision medicine implementation, disease-modifying treatments for PD may become increasingly feasible.

articles.title: Nanoparticle-Mediated Brain-Targeted Drug Delivery for Methamphetamine Use Disorder: Advances, Challenges and Translational Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Methamphetamine use disorder (MUD) poses a significant global health challenge, lacking FDA-approved pharmacotherapies. Despite extensive exploration of therapeutic targets and interventions, effective treatment remains scarce due to challenges in delivering therapeutic agents to relevant brain regions at effective concentrations. Nanoparticle-mediated delivery offers a promising approach for transporting various therapeutic cargos to the central nervous system, including small molecules, nucleic acids, peptides, proteins, and gene-editing systems. However, the application of nanomedicine strategies in addressing the unique pathophysiological characteristics of MUD has not been systematically assessed. This review presents a problem-focused analysis of how lipid-based, polymeric, inorganic, biological, and hybrid nanocarriers tackle successive delivery obstacles such as systemic stability, blood-brain barrier (BBB) penetration, brain region-specific distribution, and controlled release of intracellular cargo. We compare preclinical nanotherapeutic approaches encompassing small-molecule neuroprotective agents, anti-METH vaccines, gene-silencing RNAs, neurotrophic proteins, and emerging gene-editing methods, outlining their respective benefits, limitations, and design considerations. Additionally, we explore key factors influencing nanomedicine performance in MUD, including protein corona formation, the impact of METH-related BBB dysfunction and neuroinflammation on nanoparticle distribution, and the disparity between acute animal models and chronic human MUD with relapse tendencies. In conclusion, we present a systematic framework for aligning nanocarrier characteristics with distinct delivery obstacles and therapeutic needs. We also emphasize forthcoming avenues such as disease-triggered nanocarriers, targeted delivery to specific regions, combined nanomedical approaches, theranostic strategies, and standardized assessments of biodistribution, effectiveness, safety, and translational potential.

articles.title: Targeting NLRP3 Inflammasome Signaling After Myocardial Infarction: Mechanistic Rationale, Regulatory Networks, and Translational Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a major cause of death and heart failure despite advances in reperfusion and secondary prevention. Sterile inflammation triggered by ischemic myocardial injury is increasingly recognized as a determinant of infarct expansion, adverse ventricular remodeling, and subsequent clinical outcomes. The NOD-like receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome integrates danger-associated molecular patterns, mitochondrial dysfunction, ionic disturbance, metabolic stress, and innate immune signaling. Following activation, caspase-1 processes interleukin-1β and interleukin-18 and cleaves gasdermin D to generate the pore-forming GSDMD-N fragment, thereby promoting pyroptosis and inflammatory amplification. After MI, NLRP3 activity is shaped by extracellular adenosine triphosphate and P2X7 signaling, potassium efflux, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial DNA release, lysosomal and endoplasmic reticulum stress, and cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes signaling. Importantly, these responses are temporally and cell-type dependent: cardiomyocytes, macrophages, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts contribute differently to injury, debris clearance, vascular dysfunction, scar formation, and repair. This review differs from earlier pathway-centered summaries by integrating temporal regulation and cell-specific biology with emerging crosstalk among mitochondrial quality control, STING signaling, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and immunometabolism. Translational evidence is considered alongside mechanism, including interleukin-1-directed studies such as CANTOS and the Virginia Commonwealth University Anakinra Remodeling Trial program, while emphasizing that clinical benefit from selective NLRP3 inhibition itself remains to be established. Direct inflammasome inhibitors, colchicine, metabolic modulators, RNA-based approaches, targeted delivery systems, and traditional Chinese medicine-derived compounds are critically discussed with attention to evidence level and limitations. We further examine biomarker-guided patient selection and unresolved questions concerning therapeutic timing, cell specificity, long-term safety, and preservation of reparative inflammation.

articles.title: Postbiotics Unveiled: The Next Emerging Trend in Functional Foods.
articles.abstract: The global population is expected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, with demand for food increasing by up to 56%. Postbiotics are a safe and reliable substitute for probiotics, which are described as preparations of non-viable bacteria and/or their metabolic byproducts. Data for this narrative review was collected using Goggle scholar and PubMed from 2006 to 2026. Major bioactive compounds such as short-chain fatty acids, peptides, polysaccharides, vitamins, and cell fragments contribute to immunomodulatory, antioxidant, metabolic, and gut-brain axis effects. Preclinical and clinical research shows that they can improve insulin sensitivity, control cytokine signaling, strengthen epithelial barrier integrity, and protect against obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and depression. Postbiotics have also been found to improve mineral absorption and folate synthesis, and possess anti-sarcopenic actions. Several commercial products are available because of their health benefits. Thus, postbiotics are a revolutionary development in microbiome-based treatments; however, to completely understand their therapeutic potential, it is necessary to standardize, achieve mechanistic clarity, and ensure regulatory alignment.

articles.title: Low-dose radiotherapy ameliorates Alzheimer's-like pathology in 5xFAD mice and is associated with HIF-1α-related inflammatory signaling downregulation.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Whether fractionated low-dose radiotherapy (LDRT) alleviates Alzheimer's disease-like pathology and whether these effects are associated with microglial HIF-1α-related signaling remain unclear.
METHODS: Male 5xFAD mice received whole-brain irradiation at 2 Gy per fraction for 5 fractions (total dose, 10 Gy). One month later, cognition was assessed by the Morris water maze and novel object recognition tests, and brain pathology was evaluated by immunofluorescence and Western blot. LPS-stimulated BV2 cells were used as an in vitro model to examine the effects of LDRT on nitric oxide, cytokines, and reactive oxygen species. Transcriptomic analysis was performed with 3 biological replicates per group, followed by pharmacological validation using the HIF-1α inhibitor YC-1.
RESULTS: LDRT improved spatial and recognition memory, reduced Aβ plaque burden in the hippocampus and cortex, and attenuated microglial activation in 5xFAD mice. In particular, LDRT decreased the hippocampal Aβ plaque area fraction (P = 0.0065) and reduced HIF-1α expression in Iba1-positive microglia in the hippocampus (P = 0.0077). In addition, LDRT reduced Iba1 expression and CD68-positive area while preserving Aβ phagocytosis by primary microglia. In BV2 cells, LDRT inhibited LPS-induced inflammatory responses and altered 123 differentially expressed genes enriched in the HIF-1, IL-17, TNF, MAPK, and p53 signaling pathways. Pharmacological inhibition of HIF-1α by YC-1 recapitulated, but did not further enhance, the anti-inflammatory effects of LDRT.
CONCLUSIONS: Fractionated whole-brain LDRT ameliorates cognitive deficits and Aβ pathology in 5xFAD mice, with effects associated with downregulation of microglial HIF-1α-related signaling.

articles.title: IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis determines phosphodiesterase 1c activation inducing vascular endothelial cell damage, contributes to cerebral vascular injury and neuroinflammation.
articles.abstract: Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase 1 (PDE1) plays critical roles in mediating neuroinflammation, neuron degeneration, and cognitive impairment through suppressing the fundamental cAMP and cGMP signaling, presenting a promising therapeutic target in combating neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease. However, the crucial mechanism correlating PDE1 activation and how it regulates neuroinflammation are less studied. Here, we found that the level of PDE1c significantly increased in the cerebral tissue of cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) rats, especially of the endothelial cell population. Treating the human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVEC) with oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) or dithiothreitol (DTT) significantly increased the expression level of PDE1c at both transcription and translation levels and induced vascular cell damage. These were alongside IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis activation. Inhibition of IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis by pharmacological interventions such as TUDCA or PAIR2 or gene silencing efficiently decreased PDE1c level and ameliorated vascular cell damage. Moreover, deficiency or inhibition of PDE1c by its inhibitor PDE1-IN-4 suppressed vascular cell damage and inflammatory markers activation but marginally affected IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis. Also, no additive effects were observed when treating PDE1-IN-4 in the Xbp-1s knockdown cells. Collectively, our study revealed that IRE-1α/XBP-1s axis might be a crucial upstream regulator of PDE1c in controlling vascular endothelial barrier homeostasis, presenting a novel therapeutic strategy in ameliorating CIRI.

articles.title: Selective CB2 receptor activation attenuates neuroinflammation and preserves immune responsiveness after photothrombotic stroke.
articles.abstract: Ischemic stroke triggers neuroinflammation that can drive CNS injury-induced immunodepression syndrome (CIDS), a peripheral immunosuppressive state associated with increased infection risk. The endocannabinoid system, particularly cannabinoid receptor type 2 (CB2), represents a promising immunomodulatory target because of its anti-inflammatory actions and limited psychoactive liability. In this study, we investigated whether CB2 receptor activation confers neuroprotection and preserves systemic immune responsiveness in a murine photothrombotic stroke (PTS) model. Male C57BL/6 mice underwent PTS or sham surgery and were treated before stroke induction with the non-selective CB1/CB2 agonist WIN-55212, receptor antagonists, the selective CB2 agonist HU-308, or vehicle. Neurological deficits, infarct volume, cerebral inflammatory gene expression, and intestinal leukocyte-endothelial interactions following lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge were assessed using Neuroscore, TTC staining, RT-qPCR, and intravital microscopy. SIM-A9 microglia were used to evaluate the effects of HU-308 on viability and cytokine release under inflammatory conditions. PTS induced a CIDS-like phenotype characterized by reduced baseline leukocyte rolling and a markedly blunted leukocyte adhesion response following LPS challenge. Non-selective cannabinoid receptor activation improved neurological scores and reduced infarct size, while CB2 blockade abolished this protection. Selective CB2 activation with HU-308 reduced infarct volume, improved neurological outcome, and suppressed stroke-associated TNF and IL-6 expression in the ischemic hemisphere. In vitro, HU-308 reduced TNF release from LPS-stimulated microglia, while IL-4 enhanced microglial viability and IL-10 production. Importantly, HU-308 preserved leukocyte adhesion after LPS challenge following stroke, suggesting maintained peripheral immune responsiveness. These findings identify CB2 receptor activation as a promising neuroimmune strategy that limits acute stroke injury while attenuating the development of CIDS.

articles.title: Inhibition of Endothelial Phosphodiesterase 2A Attenuates Post-infarct Inflammation.
articles.abstract: After acute myocardial infarction (AMI), endothelial barrier dysfunction facilitates cardiac and sometimes remote pulmonary immune cell infiltration. Unraveling molecular pathways can provide targets for anti-inflammatory therapies. It is known that during bacterial pneumonia, tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α)-driven endothelial up-regulation of the dual phosphodiesterase (PDE) 2A, reducing cyclic nucleotide levels, fosters lung hyperpermeability. We studied whether PDE2A also participates in endothelial hyperpermeability after AMI. In mice, 2 days after experimental AMI, cardiac and pulmonary endothelial cell (EC) PDE2A expression was increased. This was concomitant with the induction of proinflammatory adhesion proteins and immune cell extravasation. In cultured microvascular myocardial and pulmonary ECs, TNF-α and interleukin-1β, cytokines released during cardiac ischemia, increased PDE2A expression through p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase activation. Conversely, the PDE2A inhibitor BAY 60-7550 enhanced endothelial 3',5'-cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and 3',5'-cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) levels and attenuated thrombin-induced leakiness as well as TNF-α- or interleukin-1β-stimulated vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 expression. To dissect the pathophysiological implications, we generated mice with EC-restricted PDE2A deletion (knockout). PDE2A ablation enhanced endothelial cGMP and cAMP levels and reduced cytokine-stimulated VCAM-1 expression. Accordingly, EC PDE2A knockout mice had diminished myocardial and pulmonary inflammation after AMI and reduced cardiac scarring and dysfunction. Our data indicate that endothelial induction of the cGMP and cAMP-degrading PDE2A participates in impaired cardiac and pulmonary microcirculatory barrier after AMI. Therefore, PDE2A might be a target for anti-inflammatory therapies.
